newsitem.title: USA: Quit-rate as near-term inflation gauge questioned.
newsitem.headline: Quit-rate as near-term inflation gauge questioned.

text.p: The hype surrounding the so-called quit rate in recent days was just that -- hype, as a big drop in the measure in February suggested that it is not an accurate short-term indicator of U.S. wage pressures, economists said.

After rising the past three months to 12.3 percent of the total of Americans unemployed in January, the rate of voluntary job leavers fell to 10.9 pecent in February -- its lowest level since July -- and returned to the near 11 percent level the rate has held for about two years.
"The proper interpretation (of the figure) is not to watch it month-to-month," said Steven Wieting, associate economist at Smith Barney Inc. "It's a long-term cyclical indicator."
In his Humphrey Hawkins testimony last week, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan noted the quit-rate when discussing that people aren't leaving jobs as much as in the past.
Indeed, the quit rate had risen as high as 16.5 percent by January 1990, before falling during the subsequent recession.

"Clearly, it has broken down as a leading indicator," said Brian Wesbury, chief economist at Griffin, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson Inc. "It can be a piece of evidence that the economy is close to overheating, however, in the past 16 years, it has not been a good piece of evidence."
He added that in the 1970s there was a high correlation between the high quit rate -- which was around 14 percent -- and inflation.

"Over time, I think it is important when you look at this number versus inflation," Wesbury said. "But because it is such a small portion of the overall (unemployment rate), it could be even more volatile than other pieces of data."
Those sentiments were echoed on Thursday by a Labor Department statistician and the Council of Economic Advisors chief and former Federal Reserve governor Janet Yellen on Friday.
Still, economists said that the frenzy surrounding the number was somewhat justified.
"Three increases in row can get you concerned," Wieting said. "Worker insecurity seems to be gradually deteriorating."
Confidence in the job market is purely a function of a solid economy. The longer the recovery, the more optimistic about prospects of finding a new job at better pay becomes, economists said.
Wesbury noted that the lower level of job hopping suggests employees could be getting promoted within the same company, at a better salary. That would agree with the slight rise in wages, he said.
"People," he added, "are not saying, 'take this job and shove it.'"
